period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. The battleship Petropavlovsk before her loss in 1904.

features.label: Main armament, 305 mm
features.text: Four 305-mm guns formed the main armament, two in the forward turret and two aft. Calibre is the diameter of a gun’s bore; here it was 30.5 centimetres. Twelve smaller 152-mm guns were mounted separately: eight in four wing turrets and another four in the battery.

features.label: Two funnels
features.text: The two funnels stand between the masts. Fourteen cylindrical boilers supplied steam to two triple-expansion engines, which drove two propellers. Funnels do not correspond one for one to boilers: there were far more boilers aboard.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: The forward mast carries a substantial fighting platform known as a fighting top. The after mast looks lighter. These different shapes help identify the ship in an old photograph.

features.label: Side and armour belt
features.text: An armour belt protected an important part of the side at the waterline, reaching a maximum thickness of 406 mm. This was not the thickness of the ship’s entire surface. The deck and turrets had different protection, while a mine could strike below the belt.

period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. The battleship Poltava. The exact date and location of the photograph have not been established.

features.label: Main armament, 305 mm
features.text: The main armament comprised four 305-mm guns from the Obukhov Works, two forward and two aft. The secondary guns were arranged differently: eight 152-mm guns in four turrets and another four in the battery. The small wing turrets should therefore not be mistaken for additional main-gun mounts.

features.label: Two funnels
features.text: The two funnels identify the boiler section in the silhouette. On Poltava, fourteen cylindrical boilers supplied two steam engines driving two propellers. Her sister Sevastopol had sixteen boilers, although she too had two funnels.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: The forward mast is noticeably heavier than the after mast and carries a high fighting platform, or fighting top. This feature is visible in the chosen photograph, but its exact date is unknown. The photograph cannot therefore establish the mast’s small fittings on a particular day of the war.

features.label: Side and battery
features.text: Eight 152-mm guns were mounted in pairs in four wing turrets, with another four in the battery. The secondary guns thus differed in both protection and position.

period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. Sevastopol at Kronstadt, 1900.

features.label: Main armament, 305 mm
features.text: The two large turrets at the ends of the ship each carried two 305-mm guns. Sevastopol also had twelve 152-mm Canet guns: eight in four smaller turrets and four in the battery.

features.label: Two funnels
features.text: Behind a two-funnel silhouette resembling Poltava’s was a different boiler installation: sixteen cylindrical boilers rather than fourteen. Two steam engines drove two propellers. You cannot therefore count boilers from funnels or transfer one sister ship’s specifications to another.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: Two masts can be distinguished in the chosen photograph of Sevastopol at Kronstadt in 1900. The forward mast has a fighting platform, or fighting top.

features.label: Side and battery
features.text: Eight 152-mm guns were mounted in pairs in four wing turrets, with another four in the battery. The secondary guns thus differed in both protection and position.

period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. Retvizan on the Delaware River, 1902.

features.label: Main armament, 305 mm
features.text: The forward and after turrets each held two 305-mm guns from the Obukhov Works. Twelve 152-mm Canet guns were mounted in casemates, with their crews in protected compartments of the side battery. These numbers describe the full fit at the start of the war; during the siege, some weapons were transferred ashore.

features.label: Three funnels
features.text: Retvizan had three funnels. Twenty-four Niclausse water-tube boilers supplied steam to two engines. The number of funnels helps identify the silhouette, but does not tell us how many boilers were below deck or what speed the ship could maintain after damage.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: Two substantial masts frame the group of three funnels. Their fighting platforms, or fighting tops, can be distinguished. The photograph was taken on the Delaware River in 1902, before the war and the siege of Port Arthur.

features.label: Side armour
features.text: The main belt reached 229 mm at its thickest; the same maximum is given for turret armour. These figures do not imply uniform protection across the hull.

period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. Bayan at Kronstadt, summer 1903.

features.label: Main armament, 203 mm
features.text: Bayan had only two main guns: one 203-mm gun in the forward turret and one aft. These were not the twin-gun turrets of a battleship. Another eight 152-mm Canet guns stood along the sides. The armament suited a cruiser scouting and supporting the light forces attached to the squadron.

features.label: Four funnels
features.text: Four funnels are a conspicuous feature of the first Bayan. Twenty-six Belleville boilers supplied steam to two triple-expansion engines. Designed speed was about 21 knots: a design characteristic, rather than a speed guaranteed on every sortie.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: Two slender masts contrast with the heavy military masts of the nearby battleships. The photograph confirms their general appearance and position.

features.label: Side armour
features.text: Bayan was an armoured cruiser, with a side belt up to 200 mm thick at its strongest point. The turrets had 150-mm armour. This distinguished her from protected cruisers, whose machinery was shielded chiefly by an internal deck.

period: Armament: Japanese service at the beginning of the war in 1904. Mikasa, Admiral Togo’s flagship. Illustration from a report by US naval surgeon William C. Braisted, published in 1906. The exact date and location of the photograph are not given.

features.label: Main armament, 305 mm
features.text: Four 305-mm guns were mounted in pairs in the forward and after turrets. They belonged to the Elswick/Armstrong export family, rather than being Russian guns of the same calibre. Between the main turrets was a battery of fourteen 152-mm guns; casemates protected their crews with armour.

features.label: Two funnels
features.text: Mikasa had two funnels but twenty-five Belleville boilers. Two triple-expansion engines drove two propellers; the museum gives an output of 15,000 horsepower and a speed of 18 knots.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: The forward and after masts carry fighting platforms, or fighting tops. Together with the two broad funnels, they form a distinctive silhouette.

features.label: Side and internal protection
features.text: Mikasa was intended to fight in a line of battleships, with armour protecting her sides and important internal areas. The secondary-gun casemates were separate protected compartments for guns and crews. The photograph shows their general area, but not plate thicknesses or the arrangement of protection inside the hull.

period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. The cruiser Novik at Port Arthur in 1904, according to the photograph’s catalogue attribution. The exact day has not been established.

features.label: Main armament, 120 mm
features.text: Novik’s main weapons were six single 120-mm Canet guns. Such a cruiser could support friendly torpedo craft, but had a lighter main armament than a large cruiser with 152-mm guns.

features.label: Three funnels
features.text: Three funnels suit Novik’s light, fast silhouette. Twelve water-tube boilers supplied three engines, each driving its own propeller. Average speed over the final five trial runs was 25.08 knots; an individual record should not be treated as a sustained fighting speed.

features.label: Mast
features.text: Novik had one tall mast. In the chosen photograph it stands between the after and middle funnels: an unusual and useful identifying feature.

features.label: Internal protective deck
features.text: Novik was a protected cruiser, without a side armour belt. An armoured deck shielded the machinery and other important parts from within, with sloping edges descending towards the sides. It lies inside the hull and is not visible from outside.

period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. The cruiser Varyag in June 1901, according to the photograph’s catalogue attribution. The exact location has not been established.

features.label: Main armament, 152 mm
features.text: Varyag carried twelve 152-mm Canet guns in open single deck mounts. She had no large protected turrets. Twelve was the ship’s total, rather than the number that could fire simultaneously to one side.

features.label: Four funnels
features.text: Four slender funnels appear in the photograph of 1901 and Jane’s diagram of 1904. Below deck were thirty Niclausse boilers; two engines drove two propellers. Acceptance trials produced about 23 knots, but subsequent repairs and wear mean that this figure cannot be taken as the cruiser’s speed at every moment of a battle.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: Two slender masts stand on either side of the four funnels. Their general appearance has been checked against the photograph of 1901 and Jane’s diagram of 1904.

features.label: Protected-cruiser hull
features.text: Varyag was a protected cruiser: an armoured deck shielded important parts inside the hull, while there was no heavy side belt. The deck guns remained open.

period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. Tsesarevich at Toulon, 1903.

features.label: Main armament, 305 mm
features.text: Each of the two turrets at the ends of the ship held two 305-mm guns. All twelve 152-mm Canet guns also had turrets: six twin mounts. This was an important difference from the Poltava-class battleships, where some secondary guns remained in the battery.

features.label: Two funnels
features.text: Two broad funnels stand between heavy masts. Twenty Belleville boilers supplied steam; two steam engines drove two propeller shafts. The photograph shows the ship at Toulon in 1903, before wartime damage and subsequent repairs.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: Both heavy masts carry substantial fighting platforms, or fighting tops, arranged in tiers. Together with the high sides, they make the French design easy to recognize. The photograph was taken at Toulon in 1903.

features.label: Side and torpedo bulkhead
features.text: Two armour belts protected the side, while a longitudinal torpedo bulkhead ran inside: an additional wall limiting the spread of water after an underwater explosion. It is invisible from outside. The ship stayed afloat after a torpedo hit on the first night of the war.

period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. Peresvet at Toulon, 1901.

features.label: Main armament, 254 mm
features.text: Four 254-mm guns were mounted in pairs in the forward and after turrets. Their calibre was smaller than the 305 mm of Poltava or Tsesarevich. The forward turret stood higher than the after one: the high forecastle, or raised forward section of deck, is clearly visible in the silhouette. The later Japanese armament is not shown here.

features.label: Three funnels
features.text: Three funnels and a high bow help distinguish this silhouette from the two-funnel Poltava-class battleships. Thirty Belleville boilers supplied three steam engines driving three shafts. The outward resemblance to Pobeda does not erase differences in their armament and protection.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: Both masts carry fighting platforms, or fighting tops. The after fighting top helps distinguish Peresvet’s original appearance from Pobeda’s, with her lighter after mast. The difference is confirmed by the photograph of 1901 and Melnikov’s description of the design.

features.label: Side belt
features.text: The armour belt protected the most important part of the hull, rather than the entire side equally. Coal and other loads affected how far the belt stood above water. One thickness or line on the exterior silhouette therefore cannot establish the level of protection: that requires an armour plan and knowledge of the ship’s loading.

period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. The battleship Pobeda in Russian service, between 1900 and 1904.

features.label: Main armament, 254 mm
features.text: Two turrets carried four 254-mm guns, two in each. The forward turret stood higher than the after one, on the raised forward section of deck known as the forecastle. Eleven 152-mm Canet guns formed the original secondary armament.

features.label: Three funnels
features.text: Behind the three-funnel silhouette were thirty Belleville boilers and three steam engines driving three shafts. In photographs taken from ahead, the funnels partly overlap.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: The forward mast has a fighting top, while the lighter after mast lacks a heavy platform of this kind. This is a useful difference from Peresvet. The masts partly overlap in the chosen photograph; the difference between them has also been checked against Melnikov’s description.

features.label: High side and forecastle
features.text: The forward deck, or forecastle, is raised above the after deck, placing the forward and after turrets at different levels. Pobeda shares this general feature with Peresvet. The design nevertheless evolved: Pobeda received more modern armour. An outward resemblance does not imply identical protection.

period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. Askold on trials at Kiel, 1901.

features.label: Main armament, 152 mm
features.text: Twelve 152-mm Canet guns stood on deck behind shields. A shield protected its crew only partly; it was not an enclosed armoured turret. The smaller guns were intended chiefly to repel torpedo-boat attacks.

features.label: Five funnels
features.text: Five tall funnels are Askold’s most recognizable feature. They served an installation of nineteen Schulz–Thornycroft boilers. Three engines drove three propellers. The number of funnels alone was no measure of fighting strength: artillery, protection and the condition of the machinery mattered too.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: Two slender masts stand on either side of the long group of five funnels. There are no heavy, tiered military masts like those on Tsesarevich. The photograph was taken during trials at Kiel in 1901.

features.label: Internal protective deck
features.text: An armoured deck with sloping edges towards the sides protected the main machinery and magazines from above. Askold had no continuous side armour belt. Hence the term “protected cruiser”. This deck is invisible from outside: the point on the side simply connects the explanation to the ship’s hull.

period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. Pallada in the early 1900s, before being raised and renamed by the Japanese.

features.label: Main armament, 152 mm
features.text: Pallada originally carried eight 152-mm Canet guns in deck mounts. There were no main turrets like those on a battleship. During the siege, guns and men went to land positions, so the original eight cannot automatically be taken as the armament on any given day in 1904.

features.label: Three funnels
features.text: Three funnels, two slender masts and a long hull give Pallada a family resemblance to Diana. Belleville boilers supplied three engines driving three propellers.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: Two slender masts with transverse yards frame the three funnels. This was Pallada’s appearance in the early 1900s, before being raised and renamed by the Japanese.

features.label: Internal protective deck
features.text: The armoured deck ran inside the hull, almost horizontally in the middle, with its edges sloping down towards the sides. It protected the machinery and magazines; there was no continuous side armour belt. This explains the term “protected cruiser”.

period: Armament: the original fit, with the July battle of 1904 identified separately. Diana in the Small Kronstadt Roadstead, before 1903.

features.label: Main armament, 152 mm
features.text: The original fit comprised eight 152-mm Canet guns. Six remained for the battle of 28 July (10 August) 1904: two had been transferred to Retvizan. In his account of preparations for departure, Captain Alexander Lieven noted this shortage.

features.label: Three funnels
features.text: Three funnels belong to the original appearance of the Pallada-class cruiser. Belleville boilers supplied steam to three engines driving three propellers.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: Two slender masts appear in the photograph taken in the Small Kronstadt Roadstead before 1903. It confirms the pre-war appearance, rather than every equipment detail during later voyages.

features.label: Internal protective deck
features.text: An armoured deck with sloping edges towards the sides protected the machinery and magazines from above. There was no side belt, while above-water compartments and deck-gun crews remained more vulnerable. The internal deck is invisible from outside: the point identifies the hull, rather than a particular plate on its surface.

period: Armament: the original Russian-service fit at the beginning of 1904. Boyarin flying the Danish flag on trials, 1902.

features.label: Main armament, 120 mm
features.text: Boyarin’s main armament comprised six 120-mm Canet guns in single mounts. A light cruiser’s tasks were scouting, communications and cooperation with torpedo craft, rather than fighting in the line alongside battleships.

features.label: Three funnels
features.text: Three comparatively short funnels are clearly visible in the trial photograph of 1902. Sixteen Belleville boilers supplied two engines driving two propellers. Another small cruiser, Novik, had three propellers: the same number of funnels does not imply the same machinery installation.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: The forward mast is taller than the after mast. The difference appears in the trial photograph of 1902, when the ship still flew the Danish flag. The photograph therefore supports the pre-war silhouette, rather than flags and small fittings at Port Arthur.

features.label: Internal protective deck
features.text: An armoured deck with sloping edges protected the machinery and magazines from above. There was no continuous side armour belt. A light cruiser could serve with the squadron without having a battleship’s protection.

period: Armament: Japanese service at the beginning of the war in 1904. Hatsuse in Fred T. Jane’s The Imperial Japanese Navy (1904), page 179. The exact date and location of the photograph have not been established.

features.label: Main armament, 305 mm
features.text: The forward and after turrets each held two 305-mm guns from the Elswick/Armstrong export family. The secondary armament comprised fourteen 152-mm guns. Jane’s photograph distinguishes the broad masses of the turrets and battery, but not every individual barrel and port.

features.label: Three funnels
features.text: Three funnels stand between two military masts. Twenty-five Belleville boilers supplied steam to two triple-expansion engines. Designed speed was about 18 knots; the average of 19.1 knots over four trial runs in December 1900 belongs to trial conditions.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: Two military masts with platforms, or fighting tops, frame the three funnels. These major shapes are readable in the small photograph published by Jane in 1904. Individual barrels and platform equipment are not clear enough in the photograph.

features.label: Side belt
features.text: The armour belt was up to 229 mm thick amidships; behind it, the slopes of the armoured deck gave important internal areas additional protection. Protection relied on a combination of barriers. But a waterline belt did not shield the whole underwater hull against a mine explosion.

period: Armament: Japanese service at the beginning of the war in 1904. Yashima before May 1904, according to the catalogue record. The exact location and day of the photograph have not been established.

features.label: Main armament, 305 mm
features.text: Four 305-mm Armstrong guns were mounted in pairs forward and aft. Some of the ten 152-mm guns had casemates, while the rest stood higher up behind shields. Even within one battery, crew protection differed. A similar main calibre to the later Mikasa does not imply identical mounts or ammunition-handling arrangements.

features.label: Two funnels
features.text: Yashima had two funnels and two triple-expansion engines driving two shafts. Her boilers were cylindrical. Reference works disagree on their number, so no single count is adopted here. Despite a similar two-funnel silhouette, the boiler installation differed from the later Mikasa’s.

features.label: Masts and platforms
features.text: Two military masts and low, heavy gun mounts at the ends form a compact silhouette. The archive record dates the photograph to before May 1904, without an exact day or location.

features.label: Side belt
features.text: The main belt reached 457 mm at its thickest and used Harvey armour. This does not mean that the entire side was this thick or that the ship was twice as well protected as Hatsuse. The material, area covered and entire protection scheme differed.

period: Kronstadt, 1904. View from astern before the Second Squadron's voyage.

features.label: After turret
features.text: The two barrels in the foreground belong to the after main turret. The forward turret carried another two 305 mm guns.

features.label: After mast
features.text: There is a platform on the mast. The crosspieces are yards, from which signal flags could be flown.

features.label: Funnels
features.text: From astern, one funnel overlaps the other. The top of the nearer funnel is visible, with part of the second hidden behind it.

period: Kronstadt, 1904. The battleship before its departure for the Far East.

features.label: Forward turret
features.text: The forward turret carried two main guns. A second turret of the same design stood aft.

features.label: Two funnels
features.text: The funnels stand between the masts. Their light paint and dark tops are clear in this Baltic photograph.

features.label: Mast platform
features.text: The foremast carries a platform enclosed by a railing, known as a fighting top.

period: Kronstadt roadstead, 1904. Russian service.

features.label: After turret
features.text: The after turret carried a pair of 305 mm guns. The matching forward turret is visible at the other end of the ship.

features.label: Funnels
features.text: Two funnels between the masts carried exhaust from the steam boilers. There were more boilers than funnels.

features.label: Forward superstructure
features.text: The stepped superstructure rises behind the forward turret. Its bridge gave a clear view over the deck.

period: Maizuru, 1905. After the Battle of Tsushima and before the Japanese refit.

features.label: Forward turret
features.text: The forward turret is on the left. Like the after turret, it was designed to carry two 305 mm guns.

features.label: Two funnels
features.text: Both funnels still stand in their original positions. The photograph shows Oryol before its refit for the Japanese fleet.

features.label: Visible damage
features.text: Holes and damaged fittings are visible amidships. The photograph shows what survived the battle, with no way to determine the exact time or order of the hits.
